name: Romance of the Three Kingdoms
info: Romance of the Three Kingdoms is a 14th-century Chinese historical novel attributed to Luo Guanzhong, covering the decline of the Han dynasty to the reunification of China under the Western Jin in 280, in 120 chapters.

facts.made: Attributed to Luo Guanzhong, a playwright who lived sometime between 1315 and 1400; the standard text is a recension of the 1660s by Mao Lun and his son Mao Zonggang
facts.form: A Chinese historical novel of 120 chapters, about 800,000 words, with nearly a thousand characters, mostly historical, mixing history, fiction and supernatural episodes
facts.where: Luo's 24-volume Sanguozhi Tongsu Yanyi is held in the Shanghai Library and the Tenri Central Library in Japan, among other libraries; the Mao text is the one general readers use
facts.known: The Oath of the Peach Garden; Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei; Zhuge Liang; the Battle of Red Cliffs; Cao Cao; the opening line on division and union; one of the Four Great Classic Novels

t: The novel draws mainly on Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, but adds fictional scenes, speeches and supernatural episodes, and gives its moral weight to Liu Bei and Shu Han.
Its best-known opening line, on the empire long divided and long united, was added by Mao Lun and Mao Zonggang in their recension, and none of the earlier editions contained it.
Translated first into Manchu in 1650 and later into many languages, it is regarded in Korea, Japan and Vietnam as a canonical work and has been called the national novel of Korea.
dyk: Zhuge Liang's southern campaign, which Chen Shou described in a few sentences as a single action, became seven battles in the Mao edition, in which the rebel leader Meng Huo is captured and released seven times.
ev: The Sanguozhi Pinghua, the earliest written work to combine the Three Kingdoms stories, is published sometime between 1321 and 1323
The novel is first printed as Sanguozhi Tongsu Yanyi, in an edition bearing a preface dated 1494
Zhou Yue publishes an illustrated edition in 12 volumes, with 240 two-page illustrations
A Manchu translation based on the 1522 edition, completed in 1647, is published
Mao Lun and Mao Zonggang edit the text into 120 chapters during the reign of the Kangxi Emperor
Théodore Pavie begins publishing a French translation, the first into a European language
Charles Henry Brewitt-Taylor publishes a complete English translation in two volumes
Moss Roberts publishes a full English translation with maps, a list of characters and notes

sections.origins:
Stories about the heroes of the Three Kingdoms were the basis of entertainment from the Sui and Tang dynasties, in the 6th to 10th centuries. By the Song dynasty, records mention professional oral storytellers who specialised in these tales. The earliest written work to combine them was a pinghua, the Sanguozhi Pinghua, published sometime between 1321 and 1323. Some 50 or 60 Yuan and early Ming plays about the Three Kingdoms are known to have existed, and their material is almost entirely fictional, based on thin threads of actual history.

The novel is traditionally attributed to Luo Guanzhong, a playwright who lived sometime between 1315 and 1400, in the late Yuan or early Ming period, and who was known for compiling historical plays. Its main historical source was the Records of the Three Kingdoms compiled by Chen Shou in the 3rd century, which covered events from the Yellow Turban Rebellion in 184 to the unification under the Jin dynasty in 280. Other influences include Liu Yiqing's A New Account of the Tales of the World, published in 430, Tang dynasty poetic works and Yuan dynasty operas.
sections.content:
The narrative runs from the decline of the Han dynasty and the Yellow Turban Rebellion to the reunification of China under the Western Jin in 280. It opens with corruption at court, the killing of the general He Jin by the eunuchs, and the seizure of the capital Luoyang by the warlord Dong Zhuo. Warlords then fight for territory: Cao Cao defeats Yuan Shao at Guandu in the summer of 200, and Liu Bei, with his oath brothers Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, and the strategist Zhuge Liang join Sun Quan to defeat Cao Cao at the Battle of Red Cliffs.

The novel then follows the founding of the three states: Cao Pi establishes Cao Wei, Liu Bei declares himself emperor of Shu Han as a continuation of the Han, and Sun Quan rules Eastern Wu. It tells of the death of Guan Yu, Liu Bei's defeat at Yiling, Zhuge Liang's campaigns against Wei, and the later fall of Shu and Wu to the Jin dynasty founded by Sima Yan. It has 120 chapters, about 800,000 words and nearly a thousand dramatic characters, mostly historical. Poems placed at the ends of chapters summarise events and lead to the next chapter.
sections.making:
The novel was first printed in 1522 as Sanguozhi Tongsu Yanyi, in an edition bearing a preface dated 1494, and the text may well have circulated before either date in handwritten manuscripts. Whether or not Luo wrote it, its author combined historical records with Tang poems, Yuan operas and his own interpretation of virtue and legitimacy. Luo's version in 24 volumes survives in the Shanghai Library, the Tenri Central Library in Japan and other libraries, and various recensions of 10, 12 and 20 volumes were made between 1522 and 1690.

At the end of the Ming dynasty a commentary under the name of Li Zhuowu was added to the Luo version; it was probably written by an impostor named Ye Zhou. In 1591 Zhou Yue published an edition with 240 two-page illustrations, each flanked by couplets. In the 1660s, in the reign of the Kangxi Emperor, Mao Lun and Mao Zonggang edited the text into 120 chapters, reducing it from 900,000 to 750,000 characters and removing most passages praising Cao Cao's advisers and generals. Scholars have long debated whether their viewpoint was anti-Qing or pro-Qing.
sections.reception:
The novel is acclaimed as one of the Four Great Classic Novels of Chinese literature and is arguably the most widely read historical novel in late imperial and modern China. Its literary influence in East Asia has been compared to that of Shakespeare on English literature, and many of its characters became household names in Southeast Asia. Herbert Giles stated that the Chinese regard it as the greatest of their countless novels. At the time of its publication Zhou Yue's illustrated edition was the most popular version, but the Mao recension became the standard text.

Its handling of history has been discussed since the Qing dynasty historian Zhang Xuecheng wrote that it was seven parts fact and three parts fiction. Liu Bei and his associates are the protagonists, so Shu Han is glorified and Cao Cao and Sun Quan are often denigrated, which suited the political climate of the Ming dynasty. Lu Xun wrote that Luo wished to make Liu Bei kindly but drew a character who seems a hypocrite, and that his only success was Guan Yu. Ki Taesŭng, a Korean Neo-Confucian scholar, urged King Seonjo not to read it, calling it a collection of trivial sayings.
sections.survival:
The text survives in the early printed versions and in the recension that replaced them. Luo's 24-volume edition is in libraries in Shanghai and Japan, while the Mao recension is the standard text familiar to general readers. Historical editions of the Mao version vary in the illustrations they include, and modern translations typically omit them. The 1802 edition at the Harvard-Yenching Library has 12 portrait-style illustrations, and an 1888 edition in the National Palace Museum collection has 40.

The novel also travelled by translation. Prince-regent Dorgon commissioned a Manchu translation, which was completed in 1647 and published in 1650, the first translation of the work that can be dated with certainty in any language. It was in turn translated into Xibe, Mongolian, Korean, Tibetan and French. Théodore Pavie's French version of 1845 to 1851 was the first into a European language, though only two volumes were published. English renderings began with excerpts and include Brewitt-Taylor's complete translation of 1925, Moss Roberts's abridgement of 1976 and full translation of 1991, Martin Palmer's abridgement of 2018 and Yu Sumei's translation of 2014.
sections.legacy:
The novel gave Chinese many proverbs still in use and its writing style belonged to the emergence of the written vernacular in the Ming period, with the other works known as the Four Masterworks. It has influenced literature, drama, games and popular accounts of the Three Kingdoms. Guan Yu, whom a local cult near Jade Spring Mountain in Hubei had already held as a deity, is reverenced as a Bodhisattva in Buddhist tradition, and the popularity of the novel's story of his spirit is said to have largely pushed the earlier tale of a dragon at the monastery out of sight.

In Korea it reached what has been called canonical status and has been described as the national novel of Korea. After the Imjin War its acceptance improved among all literate classes, and the Ming generals who came to repel the Japanese insisted on a shrine to Guan Yu, an episode that led to the Dongmyo temple. Fan fiction, mainly by young Chinese women, takes up the novel's plotlines and relationships. The Manchu ruler Nurhaci was said to have learned Chinese military and political strategy from it.

summary: Romance of the Three Kingdoms is a Chinese historical novel attributed to Luo Guanzhong, telling of the fall of the Han and the rivalry of Shu, Wei and Wu. First printed in 1522, it is read in the Mao recension and has been translated widely.
notes: The article contradicts itself on the Maos' edition: it dates their editing to the 1660s, but says the opening lines were added in their 'edition of 1679'. I give the opening lines as added by the Maos without a year.
Start is 1522 (first printing); the article places composition in the 14th century and Luo's dates between 1315 and 1400, with the attribution hedged.
The article's date for Peter Thoms's serialised translation ('1920 and 1921') is evidently a slip; left out.
The article says Li Zhuowu commentary was 'likely' by Ye Zhou: hedged. The Zhou Yue edition is described as '250 chapters in 12 volumes' with 240 illustrations; I give only volumes and illustrations.
The article gives the Li Zhuowu edition as 240 chapters in 120 pairs; left out as detail. Sales figure (over 20 million) is attributed to the article's 'as of 2023' statement and the year omitted.
Left out: adaptations (television, manga, games), as the brief excludes films and games, and the Buddhist claim of Zhiyi's monastery beyond what is stated.
